spatial_claims.claim: P is a point inside the circle; A, B, C are distinct points on the circumference with PA = PB = PC
O is the center of the circle; assumption that P is not equal to O
Line through O and P extended meets circumference at D and E, forming diameter DE; P lies on this diameter between D and E
P is on diameter DE and is not the center, so by 3.7 at most two equal straight lines fall from P on the circle

configuration_map: P: inside the circle (Step 1), on diameter DE between D and E (Step 3). These are consistent — any interior point lies on the chord/diameter determined by the line through it and the center. O: center of the circle (Step 2), on diameter DE (Step 3) — consistent by definition of diameter. A, B, C: on the circumference (Step 1), equidistant from P. D, E: on the circumference, endpoints of the diameter through O and P (Step 3). The configuration is straightforward: a circle with center O, a diameter DE passing through both O and the interior point P, and three points A, B, C on the circumference equidistant from P.
pass_reason: All spatial claims are mutually consistent. P being inside the circle and on diameter DE are compatible. The application of Proposition 3.7 to point P on diameter DE (with P not the center) correctly matches 3.7's hypothesis. The contradiction between three equal lines (hypothesis) and at most two equal lines (3.7) is logically valid. No angle decompositions, no between-ray claims, and no interior/exterior switches that could harbor hidden contradictions.
